issues.legal_issue: The national legislature may authorize the central government to declare a proposed route through undeveloped land as a national highway.
material_facts: The challenged declarations designated proposed highway stretches that included land without an existing road or highway.
The declarations were made under a statute empowering the central government to declare a highway as a national highway, and the proposed land acquisition was for building the highway.
issues.conclusion: The declarations were within the legislative authority of Parliament and the statutory power of the central government; the power was not limited to existing roads or highways.
issues.legal_principle: Article 246 and Entry 23 of List I empower Parliament to legislate on national highways and matters connected with them. Entries must be construed broadly, and incidental overlap with a State List subject does not invalidate a law whose substance falls within a Union List entry. Article 248 also supports Parliament’s power over matters not enumerated in the State or Concurrent Lists. Sections 2(2) and 3A of the National Highways Act, 1956 permit declaration of a highway and acquisition of “any land” for its construction, including undeveloped land. The Court relied on K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka on legislative competence and the doctrine of pith and substance, and Synthetics and Chemicals Ltd. v. State of U.P. on construing federal constitutional provisions broadly.

predicates.challenge_to_national_highway_declaratio: A proceeding challenges a declaration designating a proposed route as a national highway.
predicates.parliament_has_authority_over_national_h: The national legislature has authority to make laws concerning national highways and matters connected with them.
predicates.proposed_route_crosses_land_without_an_e: The proposed highway route crosses land on which no road or highway previously existed.

issues.definition: When a national-highway declaration is challenged, the national legislature has authority over national highways, and the proposed route crosses land without an existing road, the declaration is within legislative authority.

issues.legal_issue: The central government has executive authority to declare and construct a national highway over a route that is not an existing road.
material_facts: The challenged declarations were issued by the central government for proposed highway stretches that included undeveloped land.
The statutory provision authorizing the central government to declare highways as national highways had not itself been challenged as unconstitutional.
issues.conclusion: The challenge based on the asserted absence of Union executive power failed; the central government could declare and construct a new national highway, including over undeveloped land.
issues.legal_principle: Article 257 concerns Union-State administrative relations and does not restrict the Union’s exercise of executive power to carry out a valid law on national highways. The proviso to Article 257(2) confirms that the provision does not restrict Parliament’s power to declare highways to be national highways or the Union’s power concerning them. Sections 2(2) and 5 of the National Highways Act, 1956 support the central government’s authority to declare and develop national highways. The Court’s conclusion followed its construction of Entry 23 of List I and Article 246.

predicates.challenge_to_union_executive_authority: A proceeding challenges the central government's executive authority to act concerning a proposed national highway.
predicates.valid_law_authorizes_central_highway_act: A valid law authorizes the central government to declare and develop national highways.
predicates.proposed_highway_is_not_an_existing_road: The proposed national highway would be built on a route that was not already a road or highway.

issues.definition: When the central government's authority is challenged, a valid law authorizes its action, and the proposed highway is not an existing road, the central government has executive authority to declare and construct it.

issues.legal_issue: A reasoned policy decision by a competent expert committee to substitute a highway project is not invalidated merely because a court considers another route preferable.
material_facts: The approved national programme permitted substitution of a portion of identified stretches with suitable projects.

A committee of officials and highway experts considered regional requirements and recorded reasons for selecting the replacement route, including reducing distance and diversifying traffic from congested corridors.
The Court found the decision supported by tangible material and consistent with the programme’s policy, and found no established bad faith or manifest arbitrariness.
issues.conclusion: The substitution was a policy decision supported by reasons and material; the High Court should not have interfered with it by reassessing the adequacy of the material or the relative merits of routes.
issues.legal_principle: Judicial review of a public-purpose and technical policy decision is limited. Courts do not sit as appellate authorities to decide whether another option would be more beneficial; intervention may be warranted where the decision is mala fide, for a collateral purpose, outside the statute, irrational, manifestly unreasonable, or not genuinely for a public purpose. The Court relied on Somawanti v. State of Punjab, Sooraram Pratap Reddy v. District Collector, Akhil Bharat Goseva Sangh v. State of A.P., Union of India v. Kushala Shetty, Col. A.S. Sangwan v. Union of India, and Secretary, Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilizers v. Cipla Ltd. It also applied the principle that courts ordinarily defer to expert bodies on technical matters.

predicates.challenge_to_highway_project_substitutio: A proceeding challenges a decision to substitute one highway project or route for another.
predicates.competent_experts_recorded_public_intere: A competent committee with relevant expertise considered the project and recorded reasons connected to public needs.
predicates.decision_has_tangible_support: The decision is supported by material relevant to the project and the region.
predicates.not_proven_bad_faith_or_manifest_arbitra: The challenger has not established bad faith, a collateral purpose, or manifest arbitrariness in the decision.

issues.definition: A challenged project substitution supported by recorded public-interest reasons and relevant material is not invalidated merely through judicial reassessment of its merits if bad faith or manifest arbitrariness is not established.

issues.legal_issue: Environmental or forest clearance is not required before a highway acquisition intention is declared, but the required clearance must be obtained before final acquisition and actual construction.
material_facts: The government issued a declaration of its intention to acquire identified land for a proposed highway before environmental and forest permissions had been granted.

The acquisition scheme provided for surveys and objections after the intention notice, while the environmental process required site-specific information and applied before project construction or preparation of land, except for securing the land.
The executing agency could pursue clearance after the proposed site was identified and the land acquisition process had begun.
issues.conclusion: Prior environmental or forest clearance was not a precondition to the declarations under the highway statute or to the intention-to-acquire notice. Clearance must be obtained before the final acquisition declaration and before actual construction; the clearance process may proceed in parallel after the intention notice.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(2), 3A, 3B, 3C and 3D of the National Highways Act, 1956 establish the declaration, survey, objection and acquisition stages. Sections 5 and 11 of that Act and the National Highways Authority of India Act, 1988 govern the assignment of development work to the executing agency. The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986 and the 2006 environmental notification require clearance before construction or preparation of land, except for securing land; the 2014 Office Memorandum recognizes that land acquisition and environmental appraisal may proceed in parallel. The Court interpreted Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board v. C. Kenchappa as requiring environmental consideration before acquisition is completed, not before the initial acquisition notice.

predicates.national_highway_acquisition_proceeding: A proceeding concerns acquisition of land for a proposed national highway.
predicates.site_identified_by_intention_notice: The government has issued an intention notice that identifies the land proposed for the highway.
predicates.construction_has_not_started: Actual construction or project preparation on the land has not begun.

issues.definition: In a highway acquisition proceeding, once an intention notice identifies the site and construction has not begun, clearance need not precede that notice but must precede final acquisition and construction.

issues.legal_issue: The time spent pursuing environmental and forest clearances after an acquisition intention notice is excluded when determining whether the acquisition declaration was issued within the statutory period.
material_facts: The acquisition scheme required a final declaration within a specified period after the intention notice, subject to an express exclusion for court-stayed proceedings.
The executing agency pursued environmental and forest permissions after the intention notice, and obtaining them could consume time while the acquisition process advanced.
The Court invoked its constitutional powers to avoid making the clearance process defeat the statutory timeline and the environmental protections.
issues.conclusion: The time spent after the intention notice in pursuing environmental and forest clearances, including until those permissions attain finality, is treated as time during which the relevant acquisition action was stayed and is excluded from the statutory period.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3D(3) of the National Highways Act, 1956 provides for lapse if the final acquisition declaration is not made within the statutory period, and its proviso excludes periods when relevant action is stayed by a court. Applying Article 142 of the Constitution, the Court treated the direction in paragraph 100(1) of Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board v. C. Kenchappa as a court stay for this purpose, thereby excluding time spent seeking environmental and forest permissions until they attain finality.

predicates.national_highway_acquisition_timing_disp: A proceeding concerns whether an acquisition declaration was made within the applicable statutory period.
predicates.clearances_pursued_after_intention_notic: The government or executing agency pursues environmental or forest permissions after issuing the acquisition intention notice.
predicates.clearance_process_consumes_time_before_f: The process of obtaining those permissions takes time before the permissions become final.

issues.definition: When an acquisition timing dispute involves clearances pursued after the intention notice and the clearance process takes time before finality, that time is excluded from the acquisition period.

issues.legal_issue: An unchallenged consultant engagement is outside the scope of a challenge to highway acquisition notifications and does not by itself invalidate a reasoned project decision.
material_facts: The consultant had initially been engaged for one proposed highway stretch and was later retained for a substituted stretch.
The affected persons did not seek relief challenging the consultant’s appointment or challenge the contract for the substituted project.
The project substitution was a committee decision supported by reasons and was not founded on the consultant’s recommendation.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have expressed an opinion on the consultant’s appointment when no relief challenging it was sought; any irregularity in that appointment did not provide a basis in these proceedings to quash the project decision or acquisition notifications.
issues.legal_principle: A court should not decide an issue that is not placed in issue by the pleadings or for which no relief is sought. An alleged irregularity in a consultant’s engagement does not invalidate an independently reasoned project decision where the decision was not based on the consultant’s recommendation. The Court held that K. Lubna v. Beevi and Shrilekha Vidyarthi v. State of U.P. did not alter that conclusion in this case.

rule.if: challenge_to_acquisition_notifications and consultant_contract_not_challenged and no_relief_sought_against_consultant and project_decision_independent_of_consultant

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_notifications: A proceeding challenges notices commencing acquisition for a public project.
predicates.consultant_contract_not_challenged: The contract engaging the project consultant is not itself challenged in the proceeding.
predicates.no_relief_sought_against_consultant: The claimant does not seek a court order concerning the consultant's appointment.
predicates.project_decision_independent_of_consulta: The competent decision-maker reached the project decision independently of the consultant's recommendation.

issues.definition: When acquisition notices are challenged but the consultant contract and appointment are not, no relief is sought against the consultant, and the project decision was independent of the consultant, the appointment is outside the issue and does not invalidate that decision.

issues.legal_issue: Land records cannot be mutated in favour of an acquiring authority solely because an intention to acquire has been notified, before the land vests and possession is taken.
material_facts: Revenue entries had been changed in favour of the acquiring authority after publication of an intention-to-acquire notice.
At that stage, the acquisition process had not resulted in vesting of the land or transfer of possession.
issues.conclusion: The mutation based solely on the intention notice could not stand; the entries in the landowners’ names had to be restored until acquisition was completed and possession was taken.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 3A, 3D and 3E of the National Highways Act, 1956, an intention notice does not itself vest the land in the government or transfer possession. Vesting follows the final acquisition declaration, and possession is taken at a later stage subject to the statutory requirements.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: A proceeding concerns acquisition of privately held land for a public project.
predicates.mutation_based_only_on_intention_notice: A land record was changed in favour of the acquiring authority solely because an intention to acquire was announced.
predicates.land_not_yet_vested_or_taken_into_posses: The acquisition has not reached the stage at which the land vests in the government and possession is taken.

issues.definition: If a land record is changed solely on an intention notice before the land vests and possession is taken, the mutation in favour of the acquiring authority must be reversed.
